title: A wave travel delay raised spectral correlation but gave no clear gain over a four-hour shift at two California buoys in 2017-2020
abstract: We tested a wave-travel explanation for a prior directional wave-height forecast result at Bodega Bay and Monterey. We used NDBC spectral density and direction in 2017-2020 at eight frequencies from 0.0525 to 0.0875 Hz. The plan selected western and northern waves and compared three-hour log-energy changes with six fixed timing rules. A direction- and frequency-based deep-water group delay gave a mean correlation of 0.2535, versus 0.1349 at zero delay and 0.0427 with reversed timing. Across frequencies, the mean Fisher-z gain over zero delay was 0.1233, with conditional 95% limits of 0.1032 to 0.1435 from 28-day blocks. The gain over a fixed four-hour shift was -0.0067, with limits of -0.0168 to 0.0035. A post-plan check with reported sample minutes retained a gain over zero timing and no clear gain over four hours. One-hour log changes favored the calculated delay, while untransformed energy favored four hours. The results support a forward offset, but do not identify direct wave travel or validate the full dispersion law. Selected directions, spectral noise, approximate deep-water physics, four years and two stations limit the test. Original code, aggregate evidence, bootstrap draws, source hashes and a separate arithmetic audit are included. External source records stay outside the bundle.

display.caption: Frequency-specific correlations and timing contrasts in the planned clock-hour test. Limits use common 28-day blocks across models and frequencies.
The forward timing gain remains with reported sample minutes. The gain over a fixed four-hour shift remains uncertain.

citations.reason: Its directional bulk wave-height forecast gain leaves wave travel as an open explanation. We test spectral timing with new variables at overlapping stations and years.
Its bulk direction-interaction result does not establish wave travel. We compare fixed spectral travel delays with simple timing controls.
Established use of wave travel times and spectral observations for nearshore swell prediction. No source code or figure is copied.
